**Fed's fear meter may be pointing to stagnation, rather than**
Federal Reserve officials, who are expected to cut interest rates next week, are also moving closer to resolving a months‑long debate over the risk of stagflation after recent data showed persistent weakness in hiring and easing inflation concerns. A benchmark employment revision this week indicated nearly a million fewer jobs were added in the year through March than originally reported.  Consumer prices in August rose faster than the prior month, while initial jobless‑benefits claims jumped in the latest week, signalling a cooling labor market.  "The Fed should cut 50 basis points next week…Labor market conditions are cooling more rapidly than they were to start the year," wrote Neil Dutta, head of economics at Renaissance Macro Research.  Market analysts, including 105 of 107 economists in a recent Reuters poll, expect only a quarter‑percentage‑point cut next week, but the new data could lead officials to project a quicker and steadier drop in rates as they shift from guarding against inflation to defending the job market.  The Fed’s policy‑setting committee is expected to release updated economic projections for inflation, unemployment and the policy rate through 2028, a key mark‑to‑market exercise amid President Donald Trump’s push for rate cuts and attempts to influence the central bank, including an attempt to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook.  The last quarterly projections in June had Fed officials anticipating two quarter‑percentage‑point rate cuts this year, but seven of the 19 anticipated no moves as they weighed how Trump’s tariffs might complicate efforts to return inflation to the 2 % target.  While data this summer has eased concerns about stagflation, it has raised uneasiness about the direction of the job market.  The pass‑through of tariffs to consumer prices has been more tempered than expected, and although inflation is expected to accelerate this year, policymakers have become more comfortable with the idea that any tariff‑driven boost would be a one‑time price shock they could largely ignore.  Fed Chair Jerome Powell called that view "a reasonable base case" in remarks last month at a Fed research conference in Wyoming.  The recent benchmark employment revision points to substantially fewer job gains at the start of 2025, a key moment when officials decided to pause what had been an expected series of rate cuts this year on concern that tariffs could rekindle inflation.  Excluding two months at the end of 2024 when hiring jumped in a bout of business exuberance following Trump’s election, the revised data show job gains from April 2024 through August 2025 may have averaged just 40,000 a month, a virtual stall speed for the US economy.
